newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close mixed after curve flattening.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close mixed after curve flattening.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities closed mixed following a session of curve flattening trades on Thursday.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, as expected, did not mince words when repeating the need for the central bank to be preemptive in its battle against inflation during testimony before the Joint Economic Committee. Many market participants read his stand as hard-nosed and began pricing in a tightening of monetary policy at next Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting (FOMC).
Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc., said the market's reaction to Greenspan was interesting as it wasn't any more obvious than before which way he wanted to go.

"We'd expect to see a flattening of the curve if the Fed follows through and tightens. It's expected at this point, but it's also popular," Kretzmer said. "Most traders say they like bonds if Greenspan tightens."
Kretzmer said bonds would be popular with foreign investors, especially the Japanese -- though they would like them regardless of a few more basis points of yield.

"There's also the thought that tightening preserves the outlook for a strong dollar the rest of the year and foreigners like that too as it means more value for their dollar-denominated assets," Kretzmer said.
Josh Feinman, global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co., said he wouldn't revise his judgment of the Fed's next move based on anything Greenspan said Thursday.

"I don't expect them to move, though I've thought for a long time tightening is justified and it's coming. I'm just not convinced it'll be next week," Feinman said. "We've been in a tightening mode since last fall."
Feinman thought the Fed should have tightened monetary policy at its September meeting. Had it, it would have been a "layup" that it tightened again at this month's meeting, he said.
"They have had justification since last year and because they didn't move in September, that should throw some caution into any assessment that they will move," Feinman said.
"The market heard Greenspan say he's very close to making a decision and the market's getting very comfortable with that idea," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Glassman said market participants were contemplating any rise in rates as being an insurance policy that the current expansion could continue, that any move by the Fed would be very limited. Something to that effect may be implied in the statement accompanying the Fed's announcement.
"They kind of implied two times in 1994 that this might be it in their statements," Glassman said.
For now though, the market was pricing in a tightening and Greenspan -- keenly aware of that -- said nothing to create a little wiggle room on Thursday, Glassman said.
"I'll believe it when I see it," he said.
The Treasury's 30-year bond ended 12/32 higher at 95-27/32 to yield 6.96 percent.
Three-month bills closed up five basis points at 5.20 percent; six-month bills were up two basis points at 5.31 percent and year-bill rates ended four basis points higher at 5.50 percent.
Two-year notes ended down 2/32 at 99-10/32, yielding 6.25 percent. Five-year notes closed down 2/32 at 98-18/32, yielding 6.59 percent. Ten-year notes rose 2/32 to 96-18/32, yielding 6.73 percent.
